text: So, here I have an agent with a tool that can post Teams messages. The important question isn't just whether the agent has this tool, but when it is allowed to use it. So, first, I can allow the agent to decide when this tool is relevant. With generative orchestration, CoalPilot can choose the tool as part of working out how to complete the task. That gives it some autonomy over what to do next. But there is a separate decision about whether it can actually carry out the action without me. So, for this action, I have turned on Ask the End user before running. And I've added the prompt, I'm ready to post this update to Microsoft Teams. Do you want me to continue? That moves this action to act with approval. The agent can decide that the action is needed. It can prepare to do it, but then pause before anything actually happens. So, CoalPilot can carry the workflow forward until it reaches the point where I have deliberately kept authority. Then I can review what is about to happen and either approve or stop it. So, that is one checkpoint. But I probably wouldn't want every action to work this way. So, compare that action with retrieving information from SharePoint. So, here the agent is only reading information it already has permission to access. It's not changing a record, it's not sending a message, and it's not committing anything to anyone. So, I am comfortable letting that happen without it asking me each time. Now, of course, posting to Teams is a completely different story. That creates a visible change on my behalf. So, I may want an approval checkpoint there. It's the same agent, but with different authority levels for different actions. And that is the autonomy dial in practice. Now, approval is useful when the agent knows what it wants to do, but I still want to authorize the action. But sometimes the problem is different. Maybe the agent reaches a situation where it shouldn't make the decision by itself. For example, there could be a source that says a launch may be delayed, while another one still shows the original date. So, here I have an agent flow that pauses the workflow and asks a person for guidance. Co-pilot then sends that request to the person that I have assigned, and the workflow waits for their response and then uses that input to continue. So, this is different from simply asking me to approve an action. The system is recognizing that the situation has moved outside of the authority that I gave it, and it's handing the judgment back to me. So, you notice the difference? For routine work, I can let the system continue. For a consequential action, I can require confirmation. And for ambiguity or an exception, I can deliberately hand the decision back to a person. I don't need one autonomy setting for the whole agent. I can put human checkpoints exactly where the consequences change. So, when you design your own workflow, don't start by asking whether your agent should be autonomous. But look at the individual actions. What can it do by itself? What should require approval? And what should make it stop and ask? And that is how you turn that autonomy dial in Co-pilot Studio.
